rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The Rest of the Story
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a vast dim cavern where a huge mother dragon and a row of small dragons lie fast asleep in a heap of golden scales, a girl, a boy and an old wizard tiptoeing past with fingers to their lips, a plough horse waiting quietly behind, warm cave glow with long shadows, cozy but exciting storybook illustration

blocks.text: That evening, everyone gathered in the palace garden to hear the rest of the story. Zeb began. “After the glass city, the Mangaboos pushed us down a black stairway into the dark. We came to a place called the Valley of Voe, where the bears are invisible.” “Invisible!” gasped the Scarecrow. “You could hear them growling,” said Zeb, “and never see a single hair.” Everyone leaned a little closer to listen.

“Then we walked into a cave full of sleeping dragons,” said the Wizard. “A great mother dragon and all her little ones, snoring like engines. We tiptoed past every single tail.” “And then we met the Nome King underground,” said Dorothy. “He would not let us climb up through his kingdom. We were stuck in a tunnel with a stone wall at the end of it, and it seemed there was no way out at all.”
The friends tiptoe past the sleeping dragons.
New word: invisible — impossible to see, however hard you look. In the Valley of Voe, the bears and the people were both invisible.

“But how did you find us?” asked Zeb. Ozma smiled. “I have a Magic Picture that shows me whatever I wish to see. I saw you struggling far under the earth. So I opened a hidden road, and led you up into Oz myself.” Zeb shook his head slowly. “The middle of the earth,” he said, “is a very crowded place.” Dorothy hugged Eureka and yawned. “The strangest, longest day of my whole life,” she said, “and one of the best.”

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Great Race
chapters.artPrompt: a wooden sawhorse with jointed wooden legs racing a plough horse down a long green racecourse, dust flying from the plough horse's hooves while the wooden horse barely touches the grass, a girl and a boy cheering from the fence, an old wizard waving his hat at the start, bright festive light, exciting storybook illustration

blocks.text: One bright morning, Ozma announced a great race. Old Jim, the plough horse from California, would run against the wooden Sawhorse. Everyone in the Emerald City came to watch, and flags hung from every window. Jim looked at his thin wooden rival and shook his mane. “He is only made of wood,” Jim told Zeb. “But I was built for work, not for show.”

The Wizard waved his hat, and off they flew! Jim ran his very best, faster than any plough horse had ever run in Kansas. But the Sawhorse skimmed over the grass like a leaf on the wind. His wooden legs never tangled, never stumbled, and never once grew tired. He reached the finish flag so far ahead that he had time to look back politely. The crowd roared like the sea.
Jim the horse races the wooden Sawhorse down the course.
New word: rival — the one you race or compete against. A good race needs a good rival, and both horses had one.

Jim puffed and panted across the line, but he was not sad for long. “That,” he admitted, “is the fastest thing I ever saw in my life.” Everyone cheered for both horses, and Ozma gave Jim the cosiest stall in the royal stable. “You are a noble horse,” she told him, “for a noble try.” Jim held his head high for the rest of the day.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Eureka and the Piglets
chapters.artPrompt: a small purple kitten lying in the grass while nine tiny pink piglets tumble and climb over her, a girl in a gingham dress and an old wizard laughing nearby, an emerald palace garden with fountains, warm afternoon light, sweet storybook illustration

blocks.text: The nine tiny piglets lived with the Wizard in the Emerald City. They were pink and clean, and no bigger than your hand. Ozma loved to hold the smallest one in her palm and feel it breathe. Eureka the kitten watched them from the window seat with big green eyes. “They look like little pink sweets,” she said. “But I have learned my lesson. From now on, I shall be a very good cat.”

The next morning, Dorothy found Eureka lying in the grass with piglets everywhere. They climbed over her paws, slid down her soft back, and slept against her warm side. Eureka let them do all of it. She had decided that friends are better than breakfast, and she never once forgot it. Dorothy stood very still, so as not to spoil the game.
The piglets play all over gentle Eureka.
New word: curious — wanting to know everything about everything. Kittens are always curious, and Eureka was the most curious kitten in all Oz.

Everyone came to watch the pink heap in the grass. “You see,” said Ozma softly, “kindness grows in strange places.” The Wizard picked up the smallest piglet and tickled its ear. “Even a kitten,” he said, “can surprise you.” Eureka purred so loudly that the piglets wobbled, and everyone laughed till the garden rang.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Wizard Stays
chapters.artPrompt: a bald little wizard in a green frock coat reading a heavy book of magic in a cosy palace room, shelves of glowing bottles and curious instruments around him, green sparks dancing above his fingertips, a fairy princess and a girl in gingham watching happily from the doorway, warm lamplight, charming storybook illustration

blocks.text: One day the Wizard came to Ozma with his hat in his hands. “May I stay in Oz?” he asked. “All my life I have only done tricks. Here, I should like to learn true magic — the real kind, that helps people.” Ozma smiled at him kindly. “You rescued my Dorothy once,” she said. “Stay as long as you like, and welcome.”

So the Wizard was given a little room in the palace, with a desk and shelves and a window on the gardens. Every morning he read books of magic, and every afternoon he practised under the trees. Soon green sparks flew from his fingertips, and his old tricks began to turn into real magic. “No more circus tents for me,” he laughed. “I have found the finest circus of all — a palace full of friends.”
The Wizard studies true magic in his palace room.
New word: trick — something that only looks like magic. True magic, the Wizard found out, is different — and much harder to learn.

Dorothy visited him every day to see what he had learned. One evening he made a small green star dance around her head, and she clapped her hands. “You are becoming a real wizard,” she said. “I am becoming a student,” he said, “which is even better.” And he went back to his books, happier than he had ever been in his life.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Sightseeing with Zeb
chapters.artPrompt: a boy in simple ranch clothes leading a plough horse along an emerald city street past jewelled houses and fountains, a small purple kitten riding on the horse's back, citizens waving from balconies, green towers sparkling in sunlight, cheerful storybook illustration

blocks.text: Zeb had never seen anything like the Emerald City, so Dorothy took him to see it all. They walked along streets of green marble, past houses set with emeralds that glittered in the sun. They called on the Scarecrow, who told Zeb wise and funny things about the world. They called on the Tin Woodman, whose eyes shone when Zeb told him about falling into the earth. And they called on the Cowardly Lion, who let Zeb pat his enormous mane.

Jim the horse trotted behind them, admiring the shop windows. In Oz, animals are treated just as well as people, and Jim was given the crispest oats and the softest hay. “Back home I ploughed fields from morning to night,” said Zeb. “Here I have been patted by a lion and fed by a princess.” Dorothy laughed. “Wait till you tell them back on the ranch — if they believe a word of it.”
Zeb and Jim explore the shining streets together.
New word: marble — a smooth, polished stone used for grand floors and walls. The streets of the Emerald City are all paved with green marble.

At the end of the day, they sat on the palace steps and watched the green towers glow. “I could look at this city for a hundred years,” said Zeb. “So could I,” said Dorothy. “And soon I shall show you the rest of Oz — the strange parts, where nobody from Kansas has ever set foot.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Magic Picture
chapters.artPrompt: a tall magic picture frame glowing like a bright window in a green palace hall, a small Kansas farm with a little grey house inside the frame, a girl in gingham and a boy and an old wizard looking in with soft smiles, a kitten and a horse waiting behind, gentle golden light, tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: After many happy days, Dorothy began to think of Kansas. “Are Aunt Em and Uncle Henry all right?” she asked Ozma one evening. “Let us look,” said Ozma, and drew back the curtain of her Magic Picture. In the frame they saw the little grey farmhouse, and Aunt Em and Uncle Henry safe at their work. Then Ozma waved her hand, and the picture changed to the wide ranch in California, where Zeb had always lived.

“Everyone is safe and well,” said Ozma gently. “But they miss you, Dorothy. And Zeb — your folks are wondering where you have gone.” Dorothy looked a long time at the little grey farm. “It is time we went home,” she said quietly. Eureka stirred on her lap. “Must we?” yawned the kitten. “The palace mice are so polite here.” But she purred when Dorothy scratched her ears, for home is home, after all.
The Magic Picture shows the farm in Kansas and the ranch in California.
New word: ranch — a big farm in wide, open country. Zeb had worked on one all his life, until the day the ground opened.

“We shall go tomorrow,” said Ozma. “But remember — the belt will bring you back whenever you wish. And I shall watch for you in my Magic Picture every single day.” Dorothy hugged her. “You are the best friend anyone ever had,” she said. “Nonsense,” said Ozma, hugging her back. “I am simply a friend who is also a fairy.”

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · Good-bye to Oz
chapters.artPrompt: a farewell scene in an emerald throne room, a fairy princess holding the hands of a girl in gingham, a boy and an old wizard bowing, a scarecrow, a tin woodman and a lion gathered round, a plough horse with a small purple kitten on his back, soft morning light through tall windows, tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: The morning they were to leave, all of Dorothy’s friends came to the throne room. The Scarecrow shook Zeb’s hand and told him one last wise thing. The Tin Woodman hugged the Wizard and polished away a tin tear. The Cowardly Lion rubbed his great head against Jim’s shoulder. The Hungry Tiger purred like a small mountain, and even the Sawhorse came to watch.

“I shall stay,” said the Wizard, “and study magic. But I shall think of you every single day.” He shook hands with everyone twice, because he could not bear to stop. Then Ozma held up the magic belt. “Zeb and Jim shall go to the ranch,” she said, “and Dorothy and Eureka to Kansas. And then — a whirl of green sparkles for everyone.”
Friends gather in the throne room to say good-bye.
New word: throne — the grand chair a king or queen sits on. Ozma’s throne was made of gold and set with emeralds.

“Good-bye, Dorothy! Good-bye, Zeb! Good-bye, Jim and Eureka!” everyone called. “Come back soon!” The green sparkles rose like fireflies all around them. The last thing Dorothy saw was Ozma waving with both hands and smiling with all her heart. Then the sparkles carried them away, down and down, toward the wide, plain, lovely world.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · Homeward
chapters.artPrompt: two homecoming scenes joined by a ribbon of green light, a plough horse and a boy beside a ranch barn in golden California sunshine, and a girl holding a kitten on a Kansas farmyard path by a little grey house, sparkles fading around them, warm glowing light, gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: The green light swirled, and suddenly Zeb and Jim were standing by the big barn on the ranch. The California sun was warm on their backs, and the air smelled of hay and horses. Zeb looked around at the familiar fences. “No more glass cities,” he said. “Though I shall tell this story so many times that folks will beg me to stop.”

Far away in Kansas, Dorothy and Eureka appeared on the farm path by the little grey house. Aunt Em and Uncle Henry dropped everything they were holding and ran to meet her. “Dorothy!” they cried, hugging her all at once. “Where in the world have you been?” Dorothy hugged them back just as hard. “Not in the world at all,” she said. “And that is exactly why I have so much to tell you.”
The magic belt sets everyone down safe at home.
New word: homeward — going toward home. A homeward road always feels shorter than any other road in the world.

Eureka sat down on the familiar doorstep and washed her face, very pleased with herself. Dorothy stood in the warm evening light with the belt around her waist. Her friends were far away in fairyland, safe behind the desert. But wherever she went, she knew the way back. And knowing the way back is the best part of any journey.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · The Longest Story
chapters.artPrompt: a cosy Kansas kitchen at lamplight, a girl in a gingham dress talking with wide gestures while an older couple listens in wonder, a small purple kitten asleep on the table by the lamp, dark prairie night outside the window, warm amber light, homely storybook illustration

blocks.text: That evening, Dorothy told them the longest story of her life. She told about the earthquake, and the buggy, and falling down into the middle of the earth. She told about the glass city and the vegetable people who grew on vines. She told about the silent wooden Gargoyles and the sleeping dragons. Eureka slept through all her own adventures, purring.

She told about the trial in the Emerald City, and how everyone had said sorry to Eureka. She told about the wooden horse that outran a real horse, and the Wizard who stayed in Oz to learn true magic. Aunt Em shook her head slowly. “Well,” she said, “that child finds more weather and wonder than anyone on this prairie.”
Dorothy tells the longest story of her life.
New word: adventure — an exciting, unusual thing that happens to you. An adventure is best of all when you come home to tell it.

“And the Wizard is happy there?” asked Uncle Henry. “Happier than he ever was in a circus tent,” said Dorothy. “He says a palace full of friends is the finest circus of all.” She touched the magic belt at her waist and smiled. Wherever her friends were, Oz was waiting. And whenever she wished, the green sparkles would carry her back.
